power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support decision-making, automate tasks, personalize services, and improve system performance across domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and workplace productivity.
As AI adoption expands, clearer guidance is needed to connect human-centered design principles with measurable human outcomes.

This systematic review synthesized 44 empirical studies on human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) to examine measurement approaches, framework categories, AI roles, and domainspecific findings.
The reviewed studies showed that AI support was often associated with improved objective outcomes, including task performance and decision quality.

Subjective outcomes, including trust, satisfaction, usability, workload, and perceived control, were more variable and depended on transparency, explanation design, task fit, user expertise, and the level of human control.
Across studies, human-led AI support was the most common role, especially in high-stakes domains where humans retained final authority.
Collaborative AI appeared in tasks requiring shared activity, feedback, or adaptive support, while AI-led support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems.

Domainspecific findings showed that healthcare emphasized accuracy, reliability, and overreliance; education emphasized engagement, scaffolding, and ownership; transportation emphasized safety, timing, modality, and trust calibration; and other domains emphasized fairness, transparency, adoption, and acceptance.

This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis that connects HCAI and HAX principles with AI roles, evaluation measures, and human outcomes, supporting future frameworks that are easier to evaluate and apply in real-world settings.
that use data, rules, or learned patterns to support prediction, recommendation, decision-making, or action.
AI systems refer to tools that embed these approaches in tasks where people interact with, rely on, or oversee system behavior.
However, the adoption of AI in these domains is advancing faster than the development of clear frameworks to guide its responsible and human-centered use.
This gap creates challenges for researchers, designers, and organizations seeking to define appropriate AI support while maintaining meaningful human oversight.

In response to these challenges, human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) have emerged as important areas of research and practice, because they help define what AI systems should support and what users experience when working with those systems.
HCAI focuses on the design of AI systems that improve human outcomes while supporting human values, control, and well-being [1], [2].
text.formatted: HCAI focuses on the design of AI systems that improve human outcomes while supporting human values, control, and well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: HAX focuses more directly on the quality of interaction between humans and AI systems, including user understanding, interpretation, and collaboration with AI.
These two areas inform each other.
HCAI provides the guiding values that shape HAX design goals, while HAX findings help refine and validate HCAI principles in real-world use.
This relationship makes the two fields inherently interdependent, as reflected in Fig. 1.
text.formatted: This relationship makes the two fields inherently interdependent, as reflected in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Even with this close relationship, findings on these shared concerns remain divided across domains.
This fragmentation limits the development of shared design guidance and makes it difficult to transfer lessons across domains [3], [4].
text.formatted: This fragmentation limits the development of shared design guidance and makes it difficult to transfer lessons across domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: This issue is also reflected in practice.
According to the World Health Organization, only 8% of countries in the European Region have a dedicated national AI strategy for health [5].
text.formatted: According to the World Health Organization, only 8% of countries in the European Region have a dedicated national AI strategy for health <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: A survey by Anandarajan [6] of more than 500 data professionals also reported that 41% of companies used agentic AI in daily operations and only 27% of organizations had governance frameworks to manage and monitor these systems.
text.formatted: A survey by Anandarajan <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> of more than 500 data professionals also reported that 41% of companies used agentic AI in daily operations and only 27% of organizations had governance frameworks to manage and monitor these systems.

text.text: These findings suggest that AI adoption is advancing, while guidance on design, evaluation, and governance remains limited.
Without a unified framework, organizations may need to independently determine which decisions should be handled by AI systems and which should remain with human users.
This can lead to inconsistent design choices and uneven evaluation practices.

These problems become especially concerning in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, transportation, and cybersecurity, where poor design decisions can affect safety and the quality of human judgment.
To understand the relationship between HCAI and HAX, their roles need to be clearly defined.

Drawing on humancentered practices, HCAI can be understood as an approach to designing AI systems that enhance human capabilities while keeping the design process centered on human needs and values, with user control built into the system [7].
text.formatted: Drawing on humancentered practices, HCAI can be understood as an approach to designing AI systems that enhance human capabilities while keeping the design process centered on human needs and values, with user control built into the system <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: HCAI emphasizes systems that protect human well-being and follow ethical design principles.
It also focuses on aligning AI behavior with human values, making system actions transparent, and keeping people meaningfully involved in oversight.

Because AI systems can process large amounts of data and support adaptive decisionmaking, HCAI also enables personalization and customization, helping AI systems better serve individual and social needs.
HCAI is also closely connected to the broader tradition of human factors.
Concepts such as supervisory control, automation bias, and trust calibration are especially relevant to AI system design.
Supervisory control emphasizes the need for humans to monitor and guide automated systems.
Automation bias explains why users may over-rely on AI recommendations even when those recommendations are incorrect.
Trust calibration focuses on designing systems that support appropriate levels of trust.
These concepts show that HCAI extends beyond technical performance and considers the influence of AI systems on human judgment, behavior, and downstream outcomes.
HAX focuses on the study and design of interactions between humans and AI systems.
It examines the user's experience with AI systems, including user interpretation of system outputs and collaboration with AI.
It also considers the influence of interface features on user behavior.

In this context, HAX addresses whether an AI system is usable, whether its outputs are clear, whether its reasoning can be explained, whether users receive helpful feedback, whether people have enough control, and whether human-AI collaboration supports good decisions [3].
text.formatted: In this context, HAX addresses whether an AI system is usable, whether its outputs are clear, whether its reasoning can be explained, whether users receive helpful feedback, whether people have enough control, and whether human-AI collaboration supports good decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: In this review, HAX is used to refer to the interaction and experience aspects of human-AI systems.
HCAI provides broader design principles, and HAX examines the expression of those principles in real-world interactions and measurable outcomes.
The current body of HCAI and HAX research spans several disciplines and application areas.
Prior studies have examined these concepts in manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, education, business, and other domains.
For instance, Liu et al. [8] examined HCAI as an enabler of the transition from technology-centered to human-centered manufacturing in Industry 5.0.
text.formatted: For instance, Liu et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> examined HCAI as an enabler of the transition from technology-centered to human-centered manufacturing in Industry 5.0.

text.text: The authors introduced the HER framework, which includes human-centric design, ethical management, and responsible implications, to identify HCAI practices across 4,693 Chinese firms.
Their findings showed that HCAI can help firms balance manufacturing efficiency with human and social values.
Other studies have examined HAX design for improving work outcomes.
Krakowski et al. [9] conducted a field experiment at a pharmaceutical firm and found that tailoring HAX to match users' cognitive preferences was associated with improved sales performance.
text.formatted: Krakowski et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> conducted a field experiment at a pharmaceutical firm and found that tailoring HAX to match users' cognitive preferences was associated with improved sales performance.

text.text: This finding suggests that AI system design may be more effective when it accounts for differences in people's information processing and decisionmaking.
Similarly, Passalacqua et al. [10] reviewed HCAI research and found that psychological experiences and human factors remain underrepresented.
text.formatted: Similarly, Passalacqua et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> reviewed HCAI research and found that psychological experiences and human factors remain underrepresented.

text.text: They also identified a gap between empirical and non-empirical studies, especially in the development and evaluation of theoretical frameworks.
Transportation research has also shown the importance of human-centered AI design.

Kumar et al. [11] examined HCAI in autonomous vehicles and identified several challenges related to AI-driven human-machine interaction, including limited global standardization, trust, and data privacy.
text.formatted: Kumar et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> examined HCAI in autonomous vehicles and identified several challenges related to AI-driven human-machine interaction, including limited global standardization, trust, and data privacy.

text.text: These concerns are similar to challenges found in other domains, where AI systems support human understanding, appropriate reliance, and safe decision-making.
In addition, Vaccaro et al. [12] reviewed experimental studies on human-AI collaboration and identified factors that contribute to both success and failure in collaborative performance.
text.formatted: In addition, Vaccaro et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> reviewed experimental studies on human-AI collaboration and identified factors that contribute to both success and failure in collaborative performance.

text.text: These studies show that HCAI and HAX have been examined across many domains, and the evidence base remains difficult to compare.
Studies often use different frameworks, outcome measures, terminology, and assumptions.
Some studies focus on ethics and governance, while others focus on usability, trust, transparency, decision-making, or performance.
As a result, the field lacks a clear synthesis of which principles are most often used, which outcomes are measured, and which findings can be transferred across domains.
This limits the ability to build a shared foundation for human-centered AI design and evaluation.
Although several HCAI and HAX frameworks have been proposed, many remain difficult to apply in real-world settings.

Alelyani [13] reported that existing frameworks, including ISO 21448, Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF), and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, remain largely theoretical and require more empirical validation in real-world contexts.
text.formatted: Alelyani <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> reported that existing frameworks, including ISO 21448, Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF), and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, remain largely theoretical and require more empirical validation in real-world contexts.

text.text: This makes it difficult to apply these frameworks in dynamic and cross-disciplinary settings.
AI systems used in healthcare, transportation, cybersecurity, and education face different risks, user needs, and evaluation requirements.
At the same time, these domains also share common design concerns, such as trust, transparency, usability, safety, accountability, and human oversight.
Therefore, a key gap remains because the field lacks a shared approach for aligning AI design with human values and measurable human outcomes across domains.
It remains unclear which HCAI and HAX principles are linked to outcomes such as trust, usability, workload, safety, transparency, decision quality, and user acceptance.
It is also unclear which measures are most commonly used to evaluate these outcomes and whether these measures can be compared across application areas.
This fragmentation makes it difficult to determine which design principles are supported by empirical evidence and which principles remain mainly conceptual.

To address this gap, the present review systematically synthesizes HCAI and HAX research across application domains, with a focus on the definition, evaluation, and translation of human-centered design principles into measurable human outcomes.
Specifically, this review organizes existing frameworks, concepts, methodologies, and empirical findings to identify common patterns, shared challenges, and remaining gaps across domains.
This review has three main goals.
The first goal is to synthesize existing HCAI and HAX frameworks, concepts, and methodologies, with attention to their application and evaluation in empirical studies.

The second goal is to compare applications across domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, and cybersecurity, with attention to both shared design concerns and domain-specific constraints.

The third goal is to identify directions for future HCAI and HAX frameworks that more clearly connect design principles with measurable outcomes, including trust, usability, safety, transparency, workload, decision quality, and ethical alignment.
This review makes several related contributions.
It brings HCAI and HAX into a single review structure, allowing the values that guide AI design to be examined alongside the interaction evidence used to evaluate AI use in practice.
It also compares findings across application domains to identify where design concerns are shared and where domain-specific needs shape evaluation.
In addition, it connects proposed design principles with measurable human outcomes, which helps distinguish principles supported by empirical evidence from those that remain mainly conceptual.
This synthesis provides a foundation for future HCAI and HAX frameworks that are easier to evaluate, compare, and apply across real-world settings.
To conduct this review, we systematically identified and reviewed relevant literature on HCAI and HAX with applications in specific domains.
We categorized the literature into distinct application areas, synthesized the major findings, assessed overlap across studies, and identified variations in frameworks, measures, and outcomes.
The coded information was then organized into summary tables and visual summaries to support cross-domain comparison.
Finally, we provide recommendations for a future HCAI framework and discuss the alignment of these recommendations with existing approaches to responsible and human-centered AI design.

This systematic review was conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) method [14] to identify relevant research articles on human-centered AI and human-AI interaction.
text.formatted: This systematic review was conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) method <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> to identify relevant research articles on human-centered AI and human-AI interaction.

text.text: A total of eight databases were searched: SCOPUS, Web of Science, Compendex, Inspec, TRID, PsycINFO, ACM Digital Library, and PubMed.
Additional grey literature was searched through arXiv.
The initial search was conducted in June 2025, and all searches were completed between June and August 2025.

The inclusion criteria were articles written in English, articles published or made available online between January 1, 2010, and the final search date, and document types including peerreviewed academic journals, conference proceedings, and grey literature.

Because some online-first articles indexed during the search period were assigned a later publisher issue year, articles labeled as 2026 were retained when they were available in the searched databases before the final search date.

The syntax used to search the databases was as follows: TITLE-ABS-KEY (("human-centered AI" OR "user-centered AI" OR "human-AI collaboration" OR "human-AI interaction" OR "human-AI teaming") AND ("usability" OR "collaboration" OR "trust" OR "teaming" OR "safety" OR "ethic*" OR "interface*")).

In this article, we define AI systems broadly to include machine learning-based systems, natural language processing systems, recommendation engines, autonomous and robotic systems, and decision-support tools, provided that the system involves direct or mediated interaction with a human user.
Two reviewers searched the databases separately using the same syntax, and the larger set of results was retained to maximize coverage.
The initial search identified 9,110 records from databases and 608 additional records from grey literature sources.
After duplicate removal, 4,060 records remained for screening.
The full search, screening, eligibility, and inclusion process is summarized in Fig. 2.
text.formatted: The full search, screening, eligibility, and inclusion process is summarized in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: Two reviewers screened each paper independently to reduce reviewer bias.

Papers were excluded if they (1) lacked design principles, methodologies, applications, or impacts on human outcomes that are relevant to HCAI or HAX, (2) lacked clearly defined independent and dependent variables (IVs and DVs), (3) were review papers without original empirical data, including literature reviews, scoping reviews, or meta-analyses, (4) only compared the presence of AI with human agents without focusing on interaction or collaboration, or (5) were product overviews or interface introductions.
Of the 66 articles selected for fulltext review, 22 were excluded because they did not meet the five criteria stated above.
After study selection, the included articles were coded by domain, framework or concept, AI type, interaction modality, AI role, and reported metrics.

text.text: Section III-B summarizes the measures and metrics used to evaluate human-AI interaction.
Section III-C organizes the main framework categories and design principles.

The reviewed studies used both objective and subjective metrics to evaluate human-AI interaction.
Objective metrics mainly captured task performance, such as accuracy, error reduction, task completion time, and decision quality.
Subjective metrics captured users' experiences and perceptions, including trust, satisfaction, usability, and workload.

1) Objective Metrics: Across the reviewed studies, objective metrics most often showed that AI support improved task performance compared with baseline human performance or conventional support tools.

In Reverberi et al. [15], diagnostic accuracy increased when doctors used AI assistance, with correct diagnoses rising from five out of ten lesions without AI support to seven out of ten lesions with AI support.
text.formatted: In Reverberi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, diagnostic accuracy increased when doctors used AI assistance, with correct diagnoses rising from five out of ten lesions without AI support to seven out of ten lesions with AI support.

text.text: In Kim et al. [16], participants using LLM-assisted support for brain MRI differential diagnosis achieved higher accuracy than participants using conventional internet search.
text.formatted: In Kim et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>, participants using LLM-assisted support for brain MRI differential diagnosis achieved higher accuracy than participants using conventional internet search.

text.text: These findings suggest that AI can improve human performance in complex clinical reasoning tasks when the system provides relevant support for the task.
Performance benefits were also reported in surgical, classification, and decision-support settings.
Gao et al. [17] examined a human-AI collaborative field-of-view adjustment system for robotic-assisted surgery.
text.formatted: Gao et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> examined a human-AI collaborative field-of-view adjustment system for robotic-assisted surgery.

text.text: The system produced stable performance, lower variance, and lower NASA-TLX scores compared with several control conditions, although its task completion time did not significantly differ from manual control.
In a crowd-powered source search task, Zhao et al. [18] found that AI support helped participants locate relevant information more accurately and efficiently.
text.formatted: In a crowd-powered source search task, Zhao et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> found that AI support helped participants locate relevant information more accurately and efficiently.

text.text: In a waste-sorting task, Jacobsen et al. [19] reported that participants correctly sorted more items with AI assistance than without AI assistance.
text.formatted: In a waste-sorting task, Jacobsen et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> reported that participants correctly sorted more items with AI assistance than without AI assistance.

text.text: These findings indicate that AI support can improve task performance when it reduces search demands, organizes information, or provides timely recommendations.
Overall, objective metrics showed that AI systems often improved accuracy, efficiency, consistency, or decision quality.
These benefits were strongest when AI support matched the task, reduced unnecessary effort, and preserved meaningful human judgment.
Objective metrics also showed that AI assistance does not automatically improve outcomes.
Poor task alignment, unclear support, or poorly timed assistance can weaken performance benefits.
2) Subjective Metrics: Trust was one of the most frequently reported subjective metrics.
Across studies, trust changed based on the form of AI support, the clarity of the system output, and the user's task demands.
Chen et al. [20] found that textual explanations increased trust in human-AI decisionmaking, while visual explanations had a weaker effect on trust calibration.
text.formatted: Chen et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> found that textual explanations increased trust in human-AI decisionmaking, while visual explanations had a weaker effect on trust calibration.

text.text: Participants with higher initial trust also tended to reduce their trust after completing tasks, especially under high cognitive load.
This pattern suggests that trust is not fixed.
It can increase or decrease as users interact with AI systems and compare system support with task demands.

text.text: These findings suggest that trust is strongest when users can understand the AI output, judge its reliability, and retain control over whether to follow it.
Satisfaction was also shaped by control, collaboration, and perceived usefulness.
Satisfaction tended to decrease when AI systems limited user control or disrupted users' sense of ownership.
For example, Loske and Klumpp [25] found that truck drivers resisted an assistance system when they could not turn it off, which reduced efficiency and increased fuel use.

text.text: These findings suggest that users may value AI support less when it feels too controlling or when it weakens their sense of authorship.
Satisfaction tended to increase when AI provided support that users could accept, reject, or adjust.

Lai and Rau [27] found that employees reported stronger satisfaction when leadership support reflected human consideration or when AI structure supported task completion without becoming overly dominant.
text.formatted: Lai and Rau <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> found that employees reported stronger satisfaction when leadership support reflected human consideration or when AI structure supported task completion without becoming overly dominant.

text.text: Hemmer et al. [28] found that AI delegation increased task satisfaction and self-efficacy when the delegated tasks matched user capability.
text.formatted: Hemmer et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> found that AI delegation increased task satisfaction and self-efficacy when the delegated tasks matched user capability.

text.text: Across these studies, satisfaction was linked to users' sense that AI assistance was helpful, controllable, and aligned with their role in the task.
Usability was commonly used to evaluate whether AI systems supported effective and efficient task completion.
Across studies, usability was closely tied to transparency, controllability, and the clarity of AI support.
Cabitza et al. [29] showed that collaboration protocols and explanations can improve decision-making accuracy while also supporting critical engagement with AI outputs.
text.formatted: Cabitza et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> showed that collaboration protocols and explanations can improve decision-making accuracy while also supporting critical engagement with AI outputs.

text.text: Molina and Sundar [30] found that interactive transparency improved users' understanding of system decisions and supported stronger trust than static transparency alone.
text.formatted: Molina and Sundar <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> found that interactive transparency improved users' understanding of system decisions and supported stronger trust than static transparency alone.

text.text: Zhao et al. [18] also found that participants reported greater satisfaction when AI support helped them process information more effectively while preserving human judgment.
text.formatted: Zhao et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> also found that participants reported greater satisfaction when AI support helped them process information more effectively while preserving human judgment.

text.text: These findings suggest that usability depends on more than task success.
It also depends on whether users can understand the AI output, question it when needed, and apply it without losing control of the task.
Workload was most often measured with the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX).
Workload findings showed that AI support can reduce mental demand when it helps users focus on relevant information and removes unnecessary effort.
Gao et al. [17] found that the HIC-FoV system produced lower NASA-TLX scores during surgical field-of-view adjustment tasks, suggesting reduced mental, physical, and frustration-related demand.
text.formatted: Gao et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> found that the HIC-FoV system produced lower NASA-TLX scores during surgical field-of-view adjustment tasks, suggesting reduced mental, physical, and frustration-related demand.

text.text: Lerch et al. [31] showed that workload depended on the clarity and frequency of AI-generated interface cues.
text.formatted: Lerch et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> showed that workload depended on the clarity and frequency of AI-generated interface cues.

text.text: Low-frequency and clearer alerts were associated with lower workload, while constant and repetitive signals increased stress, effort, and sensory overload.
Explanation design also shaped workload.
Chen et al. [20] found that textual explanations improved trust and perceived reliability but increased cognitive load and performed worse under time pressure.
text.formatted: Chen et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> found that textual explanations improved trust and perceived reliability but increased cognitive load and performed worse under time pressure.

text.text: These findings show that AI assistance does not automatically reduce workload.

Workload improves when the system provides clear support at the right time, and workload can increase when explanations or cues add information that users need to process during an already demanding task.
Overall, subjective metrics showed that users' experiences with AI depend strongly on transparency, control, task fit, and interaction design.
Trust, satisfaction, usability, and workload were closely connected rather than independent outcomes.
A system that improves performance may still create a poor user experience if it increases mental demand, reduces perceived control, or encourages blind reliance.
The 44 included studies were organized into eight framework categories based on their main conceptual focus.

These categories included automation and human control, initiative dynamics, affective and engagement orientation, cognitive support, fairness, trust, personalization and adaptivity, and technology adoption with human performance.

This categorization shows that current HCAI and HAX frameworks focus most strongly on control, collaboration, trust, and explainability, while broader adoption and long-term implementation remain less represented.
Automation and human control was the most common framework category (n = 10).
This emphasis reflects a central concern in HCAI: AI systems should improve performance while preserving meaningful human oversight.
For example, Huang et al. [32] proposed a triadic human-AI collaboration framework for autonomous mobility.
text.formatted: For example, Huang et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> proposed a triadic human-AI collaboration framework for autonomous mobility.

text.text: In this framework, Advisor AI provides context-aware information without taking control, Co-pilot AI shares control with the human user, and Guardian AI acts as a safety override during emergencies.
This framework shows a graded view of AI support, with different levels of control depending on task risk and user need.
Other studies also emphasized the balance between automation and human control.
Van der Waa et al. [33] proposed team design patterns for morally complex decision-making, ranging from human decision-making with AI advice to supervised autonomy.
text.formatted: Van der Waa et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> proposed team design patterns for morally complex decision-making, ranging from human decision-making with AI advice to supervised autonomy.

text.text: Batra et al. [34] applied Shneiderman's HCAI framework to examine personal control and automation in AI agents.
text.formatted: Batra et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> applied Shneiderman's HCAI framework to examine personal control and automation in AI agents.

text.text: Hemmer et al. [28] and Gal et al. [35] examined AI delegation and task allocation, where AI systems routed tasks based on confidence or task difficulty.
text.formatted: Hemmer et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> and Gal et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> examined AI delegation and task allocation, where AI systems routed tasks based on confidence or task difficulty.

text.text: Across these studies, the main design concern was not whether AI should be used, but which task elements should remain with humans and which should be supported or handled by AI.
Initiative dynamics formed another major framework category (n = 6).
These studies examined whether humans or AI systems should act first, respond second, or shift initiative during the task.
Initiative shaped task performance, perceived AI competence, responsibility, and trust.
For instance, Schecter and Richardson [36] examined generative AI as either a driver or an advisor.
text.formatted: For instance, Schecter and Richardson <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> examined generative AI as either a driver or an advisor.

text.text: When AI acted as the driver, it produced an initial solution that humans refined.
When AI acted as the advisor, humans worked first and then received AI critique or suggestions.
Cabitza et al. [29] also compared different human-AI collaboration protocols, including AI-first and human-first configurations.
text.formatted: Cabitza et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> also compared different human-AI collaboration protocols, including AI-first and human-first configurations.

text.text: These studies show that the order of human and AI input can meaningfully shape performance and user perception, even when the same AI system is used.
Affective and engagement-oriented frameworks appeared in three studies.
These frameworks focused on emotional response, motivation, and user engagement.
For example, Gal et al. [35] used motivational messages to support participation in a citizen science workflow.
text.formatted: For example, Gal et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> used motivational messages to support participation in a citizen science workflow.

text.text: Song et al. [37] used cooperative chatbot interaction to influence engagement and attitudes toward mental illness.
text.formatted: Song et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref> used cooperative chatbot interaction to influence engagement and attitudes toward mental illness.

text.text: These studies suggest that HCAI and HAX frameworks should account for users' emotional and motivational responses, especially in learning, health communication, and public-facing systems.
Cognitive support frameworks appeared in two studies.
These frameworks focused on helping users evaluate AI outputs more carefully and avoid shallow reliance.
For example, Chen et al. [20] examined cognitive framework features such as explanations, confidence information, feedback, AI-driven questions, and performance visualization.
text.formatted: For example, Chen et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> examined cognitive framework features such as explanations, confidence information, feedback, AI-driven questions, and performance visualization.

text.text: These features were intended to slow automatic judgment and encourage more reflective decision-making.
Cognitive support is especially important when AI systems provide recommendations in highstakes tasks where users may over-rely on system outputs.
Fairness frameworks appeared in two studies, both in HR or technology-related contexts.
These studies focused on fairness perceptions in AI-assisted hiring and decision-making.

For instance, Ling et al. [38] examined AI-led, balanced, and human-led screening structures and found that applicants perceived human-led and balanced structures as fairer than AI-led structures, especially when the outcome was rejection.
text.formatted: For instance, Ling et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> examined AI-led, balanced, and human-led screening structures and found that applicants perceived human-led and balanced structures as fairer than AI-led structures, especially when the outcome was rejection.

text.text: This finding suggests that perceived fairness depends on both the outcome and the decision process, including the relative weight given to humans and AI.
Personalization and adaptivity appeared in two studies.
These frameworks examined AI systems that adjusted to user behavior, task context, or environmental conditions.
For example, Lerch et al. [31] evaluated generated user interfaces in automated vehicles that adapted notifications based on motion-sicknessrelated conditions.
text.formatted: For example, Lerch et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> evaluated generated user interfaces in automated vehicles that adapted notifications based on motion-sicknessrelated conditions.

text.text: Adaptive systems were often perceived as useful when they responded to the user's situation, yet they could also increase workload when cues were repetitive or unclear.
This pattern suggests that adaptivity needs to be guided by user needs, task timing, and information clarity.
Trust frameworks appeared in three studies.
These studies focused on trust calibration, overtrust, undertrust, and reliance.
For example, Okamura and Yamada [24] proposed adaptive trust calibration cues that appeared when user behavior suggested overtrust.
text.formatted: For example, Okamura and Yamada <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> proposed adaptive trust calibration cues that appeared when user behavior suggested overtrust.

text.text: The cues helped users adjust their reliance when AI reliability changed.
Trust frameworks were closely connected to transparency and control because users needed enough information to judge whether AI support should be accepted.
Technology adoption and human performance appeared in one study.
Loske and Klumpp [25] examined professional truck drivers' responses to assistance systems with different levels of controllability.
text.formatted: Loske and Klumpp <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> examined professional truck drivers' responses to assistance systems with different levels of controllability.

text.text: Their findings showed that adoption depends on more than perceived usefulness.
Users also need meaningful control and the option to override or disengage from automation.
The limited number of studies in this category suggests that future HCAI and HAX research should place more attention on adoption, long-term use, and real-world implementation.
Across the framework categories, automation and human control received the most attention, while adoption and longterm performance received less attention.

This imbalance shows that the field has made progress in defining design principles, but less progress in testing whether those principles support sustainable and transferable human outcomes across domains.
The included studies were also organized by the role AI played in human-AI interaction.
Three broad role categories were identified: human-led AI support, human-AI collaborative support, and AI-led support.
Human-led support refers to systems that provide information, recommendations, explanations, or decision support while humans retain final authority.
Human-AI collaborative support refers to systems that share control, exchange feedback, or coordinate task activity with humans.
AI-led support refers to systems that initiate or complete tasks with minimal human input.
Several studies included mixed-role systems where AI shifted between these roles depending on context, task demands, or risk level.
Human-led AI support was the most common role across the reviewed studies.
This pattern reflects the strong presence of high-stakes domains such as healthcare, transportation, and HR, where final responsibility often remains with human users.
Collaborative support appeared when tasks required ongoing coordination between humans and AI.
AI-led support rarely appeared as a stand-alone role.
Instead, it most often appeared as part of mixed-role systems in which AI could act autonomously under some conditions and provide support under others.
1) Human-led AI Support: Human-led AI support appeared most frequently across the included articles.
In this role, AI mainly functions as an assistant that provides information or recommendations without directly taking final control.
Clinical diagnosis was a common example.
In Niraula et al. [39], AI provided treatment suggestions based on cancer progression, while clinicians reviewed the suggestions and decided whether to follow, revise, or reject them.
text.formatted: In Niraula et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>, AI provided treatment suggestions based on cancer progression, while clinicians reviewed the suggestions and decided whether to follow, revise, or reject them.

text.text: In Reverberi et al. [15], endoscopists integrated their own judgments with AI outputs when diagnosing colonoscopy lesions.
text.formatted: In Reverberi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, endoscopists integrated their own judgments with AI outputs when diagnosing colonoscopy lesions.

text.text: In Cabitza et al. [40], AI acted as an additional reader in radiology, and its judgments were combined with radiologists' judgments under different collaboration protocols.
text.formatted: In Cabitza et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref>, AI acted as an additional reader in radiology, and its judgments were combined with radiologists' judgments under different collaboration protocols.

text.text: Human-led AI support also appeared in patient-facing healthcare.
Sayres et al. [41] examined a dermatology application that helped users compare their own skin concerns with visual examples and AI-supported information.
text.formatted: Sayres et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> examined a dermatology application that helped users compare their own skin concerns with visual examples and AI-supported information.

text.text: In this case, AI supported patients' understanding and also helped clinicians communicate with patients.
This example shows that humanled AI support can assist expert users, lay users, or both groups within the same care process.
Outside healthcare, advisory AI appeared in decision-making, transportation, and work tasks.
Smith et al. [23] examined AI advice in facial recognition decisions, where participants could decide whether to follow or reject the AI recommendation.
text.formatted: Smith et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> examined AI advice in facial recognition decisions, where participants could decide whether to follow or reject the AI recommendation.

text.text: Lee and Tok [42] examined AI predictions, uncertainty scores, visualizations, and example-based explanations in rehabilitation assessment.
text.formatted: Lee and Tok <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref> examined AI predictions, uncertainty scores, visualizations, and example-based explanations in rehabilitation assessment.

text.text: Lerch et al. [31] examined an in-vehicle AIgenerated interface that notified users about upcoming curvy roads linked to motion sickness risk.
text.formatted: Lerch et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> examined an in-vehicle AIgenerated interface that notified users about upcoming curvy roads linked to motion sickness risk.

text.text: Across these examples, AI supported the user's decision rather than replacing it.
Explainability was a recurring feature of human-led AI support.
Because humans retained final control, the AI needed to provide enough information for users to judge the recommendation.
Chen et al. [20] examined text explanations, visual explanations, confidence levels, feedback, AI-driven questions, and performance visualizations in diabetes management.
text.formatted: Chen et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> examined text explanations, visual explanations, confidence levels, feedback, AI-driven questions, and performance visualizations in diabetes management.

text.text: Senoner et al. [43] compared a black-box AI system with an explainable AI system that used heatmaps during a visual inspection task.
text.formatted: Senoner et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43]</ref> compared a black-box AI system with an explainable AI system that used heatmaps during a visual inspection task.

text.text: Schmitt et al. [44] examined salient feature explanations and free-text explanations in disinformation detection.
text.formatted: Schmitt et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref> examined salient feature explanations and free-text explanations in disinformation detection.

text.text: These studies show that human-led AI support often depends on explanation quality because users need to understand the AI output before deciding whether to rely on it.
Overall, human-led AI support was most common when users needed to process complex information, make final judgments, or remain accountable for decisions.

This role supports HCAI principles by preserving human authority, while HAX findings show that the quality of explanations, timing, and presentation strongly affects user trust, reliance, and performance.
2) Human-AI Collaborative Support: Human-AI collaborative support reflects a shift from advice to shared task activity.
In this role, AI systems interact with users more actively, respond to context, and share parts of the task.
Gao et al. [17], for example, examined a surgical field-of-view adjustment system that interpreted surgical scenes and responded to surgeons' voice commands.
text.formatted: Gao et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, for example, examined a surgical field-of-view adjustment system that interpreted surgical scenes and responded to surgeons' voice commands.

text.text: The system helped stabilize the view and reduced workload, while the surgeon remained actively involved in the procedure.
This example shows collaborative support in a high-skill setting where AI helps manage task demands without removing the human operator.
Collaborative AI also appeared in writing, rehabilitation, ethics, learning, and emergency response.
Dhillon et al. [26] examined AI scaffolding in co-writing, where AI provided next-sentence or next-paragraph support.
text.formatted: Dhillon et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> examined AI scaffolding in co-writing, where AI provided next-sentence or next-paragraph support.

text.text: Hemmer et al. [28] examined AI delegation in image classification, where AI routed task instances to humans or handled them automatically.
text.formatted: Hemmer et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> examined AI delegation in image classification, where AI routed task instances to humans or handled them automatically.

text.text: Schwalb et al. [45] examined a drone-based AI system that detected hostages and communicated findings through a visual interface.
text.formatted: Schwalb et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[45]</ref> examined a drone-based AI system that detected hostages and communicated findings through a visual interface.

text.text: These systems did more than present advice; they participated in task coordination and shaped the flow of human activity.
A key feature of collaborative AI was contextual alignment.
Effective systems interpreted task conditions, user input, or environmental cues and then provided support that matched the situation.
In education, Gyasi et al. [46] examined AI systems that provided feedback, feedforward, and chatbot partnership during collaborative learning.
text.formatted: In education, Gyasi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref> examined AI systems that provided feedback, feedforward, and chatbot partnership during collaborative learning.

text.text: In this case, AI became part of the learning process rather than a separate tool.
In Batra et al. [34], AI agents were discussed as systems that could support safety, auditability, fairness, and oversight.
text.formatted: In Batra et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>, AI agents were discussed as systems that could support safety, auditability, fairness, and oversight.

text.text: These examples show that collaborative AI can support both task activity and broader governance goals.
Overall, human-AI collaborative support was most useful when the task required ongoing coordination, adaptive feedback, or shared control.
This role helps connect HCAI and HAX because it requires both value-based design principles and careful evaluation of interaction quality during use.
3) AI-Led Support and Mixed-Role Systems: No included study focused only on AI-led support as a stand-alone role.
AIled support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems where AI could shift among advisory, collaborative, and automated functions.
This pattern is important because it suggests that empirical HCAI and HAX research has not centered on full AI replacement.
Instead, most studies examined AI systems that changed their level of involvement based on task context, risk, or user control.
Several studies combined human-led and collaborative AI roles.
For example, Gyasi et al. [46] compared AI feedforward and feedback, AI partnership, and a combined mode in online collaborative learning.
text.formatted: For example, Gyasi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref> compared AI feedforward and feedback, AI partnership, and a combined mode in online collaborative learning.

text.text: Brachman et al. [47] examined conflict resolution in data labeling, where participants could rely on human labeler agreement, AI probability, or both.
text.formatted: Brachman et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[47]</ref> examined conflict resolution in data labeling, where participants could rely on human labeler agreement, AI probability, or both.

text.text: Cabitza et al. [40] compared workflows in which humans led first, AI led first, or disagreements were resolved through structured protocols.
text.formatted: Cabitza et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> compared workflows in which humans led first, AI led first, or disagreements were resolved through structured protocols.

text.text: Schecter and Richardson [36] compared AI as a driver and AI as an advisor in generative AI-supported work.
text.formatted: Schecter and Richardson <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> compared AI as a driver and AI as an advisor in generative AI-supported work.

text.text: These studies show that AI roles can shift during interaction rather than remain fixed.
Some studies combined collaborative and AI-led roles.
Madathil [48] compared human-AI-generated advertisements with fully AI-generated advertisements.
text.formatted: Madathil <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[48]</ref> compared human-AI-generated advertisements with fully AI-generated advertisements.

text.text: Li and Kang [49] compared human-centered AI with machine-centered AI in retail, where AI could personalize services or automate task operations.
text.formatted: Li and Kang <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref> compared human-centered AI with machine-centered AI in retail, where AI could personalize services or automate task operations.

text.text: Loske and Klumpp [25] compared assistance systems that could be controlled by drivers with systems that could not be turned off.
text.formatted: Loske and Klumpp <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> compared assistance systems that could be controlled by drivers with systems that could not be turned off.

text.text: Across these studies, users responded more positively when AI support preserved meaningful human involvement.
A small set of studies included all three roles.
In automated driving, advisory AI could inform drivers, collaborative AI could provide stronger adaptive support, and AI-led support could intervene during unsafe conditions [32], [50].
text.formatted: In automated driving, advisory AI could inform drivers, collaborative AI could provide stronger adaptive support, and AI-led support could intervene during unsafe conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref>.

text.text: Zhao et al. [18] also showed a workflow in which AI searched autonomously, provided candidate solutions, and handed control to humans when needed.
text.formatted: Zhao et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> also showed a workflow in which AI searched autonomously, provided candidate solutions, and handed control to humans when needed.

text.text: These studies suggest that mixed-role systems may be especially relevant in dynamic environments where risk and task demands change over time.

Across AI roles, the main pattern was clear: users often accepted AI support when it strengthened decision-making, reduced effort, or improved safety, but they were less accepting when AI removed control or made decisions difficult to question.
This finding supports the need for HCAI and HAX frameworks that specify not just what AI can do, but when AI should advise, collaborate, or act.
E. Domain-Specific Findings 1) Healthcare: Healthcare was the largest domain in the review, with 12 included studies.
The healthcare studies focused mainly on decision support, diagnostic support, surgical assistance, and knowledge adoption.
Across these studies, AI was most often used to support human judgment in highstakes tasks where accuracy, reliability, and accountability were important.
Decision support was a major theme in healthcare.
AI systems supported tasks such as diabetes management, rehabilitation assessment, adaptive radiotherapy, dietetics planning, and resource allocation during public health emergencies.
Across these studies, explainable AI was commonly used to help users interpret recommendations.
Explanations appeared as confidence scores, visual indicators, text explanations, counterfactual explanations, uncertainty information, and contrastive explanations.
These explanation formats were intended to help users judge whether AI outputs were reliable and relevant to the task.
Confidence information was one common form of explainable AI.
For instance, Lee and Tok [42] compared numerical confidence scores with distance-based confidence information in rehabilitation assessment.
text.formatted: For instance, Lee and Tok <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref> compared numerical confidence scores with distance-based confidence information in rehabilitation assessment.

text.text: Distance-based confidence information improved accuracy, especially for novices, while numerical confidence scores were often preferred by users.
This finding shows that the explanation format users prefer may not always be the format that produces the strongest performance.
Textual and visual explanations were also common.

Chen et al. [20] found that textual explanations improved trust and perceived reliability in high-stakes healthcare decision-making, but they could increase cognitive load and perform less well under time pressure.
text.formatted: Chen et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> found that textual explanations improved trust and perceived reliability in high-stakes healthcare decision-making, but they could increase cognitive load and perform less well under time pressure.

text.text: Visual explanations improved satisfaction and perceived accuracy in some cases, yet they did not consistently improve reliance calibration or performance.
Lee and Chew [51] showed that counterfactual explanations helped reduce overreliance on incorrect AI outputs.
text.formatted: Lee and Chew <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51]</ref> showed that counterfactual explanations helped reduce overreliance on incorrect AI outputs.

text.text: Van der Waa et al. [33] showed that contrastive explanations could support moral decision-making by explaining why one allocation decision was favored over another.
text.formatted: Van der Waa et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> showed that contrastive explanations could support moral decision-making by explaining why one allocation decision was favored over another.

text.text: These findings suggest that XAI can support decision-making, but its effects depend on explanation type, task pressure, and user expertise.
Expertise was an important factor in healthcare decision support.
Several studies found that novices and experts both benefited from AI support, but they responded differently to incorrect AI outputs.
Novices often showed larger performance gains when AI was correct, yet they were more vulnerable to incorrect AI recommendations.
Experts sometimes took longer when working with AI, but they were less affected by erroneous outputs.
This pattern suggests that AI explanations should be designed differently for novice and expert users, especially in clinical tasks where overreliance can affect patient outcomes.
Diagnostic support was another major healthcare application.
Studies examined MRI, ECG, X-ray, colonoscopy, and skin condition diagnosis.
Across these tasks, human-AI collaboration often improved diagnostic accuracy and was perceived as useful, consistent, or satisfying.
Cabitza et al. [29] showed that welldesigned human-AI collaboration protocols could outperform either humans or AI alone.
text.formatted: Cabitza et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> showed that welldesigned human-AI collaboration protocols could outperform either humans or AI alone.

text.text: Senoner et al. [43] found that visual heatmap explanations improved performance in medical and manufacturing tasks.
text.formatted: Senoner et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43]</ref> found that visual heatmap explanations improved performance in medical and manufacturing tasks.

text.text: Sayres et al. [41] showed that AI support could help patients better understand skin concerns and support communication with clinicians.
text.formatted: Sayres et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> showed that AI support could help patients better understand skin concerns and support communication with clinicians.

text.text: These findings suggest that diagnostic AI is most useful when it supports interpretation, communication, and final human judgment.
Surgical support appeared in Gao et al. [17], which examined an AI-powered surgical field-of-view adjustment assistant.
text.formatted: Surgical support appeared in Gao et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, which examined an AI-powered surgical field-of-view adjustment assistant.

text.text: The system interpreted the surgical scene and surgeon intent, then adjusted the field of view to support the task.
The system reduced workload and supported stable performance, suggesting that collaborative AI can help manage complex perceptual and motor demands in surgical settings.
One study examined knowledge adoption in chronic disease prevention.
Lu and Peng [52] compared factual, interpretive, and exploratory tasks.
text.formatted: Lu and Peng <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[52]</ref> compared factual, interpretive, and exploratory tasks.

text.text: Participants performed best on interpretive tasks and lowest on factual tasks, suggesting that AIsupported knowledge work may be most useful when users need to interpret and apply information rather than simply recall facts.
Overall, healthcare studies showed strong potential for HCAI and HAX because AI often improved accuracy, efficiency, and decision support.
The same studies also showed clear risks, especially overreliance, explanation burden, and different effects for novice and expert users.
Healthcare findings therefore show the need for AI systems that are accurate, explainable, and designed around the user's role, expertise, and level of responsibility.
2) Education: Five studies examined HCAI and HAX in education.
A common theme was engagement.
Across the education studies, AI systems were more effective when they supported active participation, meaningful interaction, and task-relevant scaffolding [26], [35], [37], [46], [53].
text.formatted: Across the education studies, AI systems were more effective when they supported active participation, meaningful interaction, and task-relevant scaffolding <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref>.

text.text: Song et al. [37] examined chatbot interaction in the context of mental illness stigma.
text.formatted: Song et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref> examined chatbot interaction in the context of mental illness stigma.

text.text: Two-way cooperative interaction helped participants view the chatbot as more intelligent and likable, and it supported stronger engagement.
The effects were strongest when the chatbot activity was tied directly to mental illness content.
When the cooperative task was not connected to the mental illness content, participants did not report a sense of cooperation.
This finding suggests that educational AI should support interaction that is meaningful for the learning goal.
Gyasi et al. [46] further showed the value of active AI support in collaborative learning.
text.formatted: Gyasi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref> further showed the value of active AI support in collaborative learning.

text.text: The combined AIFFP condition, which included feedforward, feedback, and an AI partner, produced the strongest collaborative knowledge building, cognitive engagement, and socially shared regulation.
This condition outperformed AI feedback alone and AI partnership alone.
These results suggest that AI support is most useful when it gives learners task-specific guidance and also participates in the learning process.
Kim and Lee [53], examined student-AI collaboration in a drawing task.
text.formatted: Kim and Lee <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref>, examined student-AI collaboration in a drawing task.

text.text: Students who framed the problem first, including goals, constraints, and options, showed larger creativity gains than students who began drawing immediately.
The findings also showed that student attitude and skill level shaped the effect of AI support.
Students with different skill levels wanted different forms of guidance, suggesting that educational AI should provide adaptive scaffolding rather than a single fixed level of automation.
Furthermore, Dhillon et al. [26] examined AI scaffolding in co-writing.
text.formatted: Furthermore, Dhillon et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> examined AI scaffolding in co-writing.

text.text: Low-level sentence guidance did not significantly improve writing quality or productivity, while higher-level paragraph guidance produced significant improvement, especially for writers without a regular writing habit.
The study also showed a moderate decrease in satisfaction and text ownership under scaffolded writing.
This finding suggests that educational AI should match the level of scaffolding to the writer and support performance without weakening the user's sense of ownership.
Overall, education studies showed that AI can support engagement, performance, and collaborative learning when it provides task-relevant feedback and adaptive scaffolding.
The main risk is that AI can reduce ownership, disrupt learning flow, or create dependence when the level of support is poorly matched to the learner.
Five studies examined HCAI and HAX in transportation.
The main themes were adaptive interfaces, interaction modalities, technology adoption, user control, and explainable AI.
These studies were often concerned with safety, timing, trust, and the need for fast user response in dynamic environments.
Adaptive interfaces were a major theme.
Bellet et al. [50] examined adaptive human-machine transitions in vehicle automation, where the system monitored driver behavior and situational risk to guide information, warning, or intervention.
