text.text: Lerch et al. [31] examined AI-generated motion sickness notifications in automated vehicles.
text.formatted: Lerch et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> examined AI-generated motion sickness notifications in automated vehicles.

text.text: Kaufman [54] examined AI coaching for autonomous vehicle interaction.
text.formatted: Kaufman <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> examined AI coaching for autonomous vehicle interaction.

text.text: Across these studies, adaptive interfaces were useful when they responded to the driving context and provided timely support.
Users often rated these systems as helpful, intuitive, and safe when the information was clear and well timed.
Interaction modality was another important transportation theme.
Visual, auditory, tactile, and multimodal cues were used to support driver understanding and response.
Huang et al. [32] and Kaufman [54] examined how information format and modality shape user experience in driving contexts.
text.formatted: Huang et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> and Kaufman <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> examined how information format and modality shape user experience in driving contexts.

text.text: In Huang et al. [32], the Advisor, Co-pilot, and Guardian roles, delivered through visual, auditory, and tactile channels, were rated as equally useful and satisfying.
text.formatted: In Huang et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>, the Advisor, Co-pilot, and Guardian roles, delivered through visual, auditory, and tactile channels, were rated as equally useful and satisfying.

text.text: In Kaufman [54], visual-spatial cues combined with auditory reasoning provided the best user experience in a driving coaching context.
text.formatted: In Kaufman <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref>, visual-spatial cues combined with auditory reasoning provided the best user experience in a driving coaching context.

text.text: These findings suggest that transportation AI should match modality and information type to the task demand, urgency, and driver state.
User control and adoption were also central.
Bellet et al. [50] and Loske and Klumpp [25] showed that users were more accepting of assistance systems when they retained meaningful control.
text.formatted: Bellet et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref> and Loske and Klumpp <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> showed that users were more accepting of assistance systems when they retained meaningful control.

text.text: Loske and Klumpp [25], in particular, found that drivers resisted systems that could not be turned off, which led to poorer efficiency.
text.formatted: Loske and Klumpp <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>, in particular, found that drivers resisted systems that could not be turned off, which led to poorer efficiency.

text.text: This finding suggests that user control is not only a preference.
It can affect real performance outcomes such as fuel use and driving efficiency.
Explainable AI also appeared in transportation.
Kaufman [54] showed that AI coaching improved driving performance, confidence, expertise, and trust, and that modality and expla-nation type significantly affected learning effectiveness.
text.formatted: Kaufman <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> showed that AI coaching improved driving performance, confidence, expertise, and trust, and that modality and expla-nation type significantly affected learning effectiveness.

text.text: This finding is especially important for transportation because trust needs to be calibrated under time pressure and safety risk, and explanation design can shape whether drivers rely on AI support appropriately.
Overall, transportation studies showed that HCAI and HAX design needs to support timely communication, clear modality selection, calibrated trust, and meaningful human control.
These concerns are especially important in automated driving because users need to understand AI support quickly and decide whether to rely on it during changing traffic conditions.

The remaining studies covered HR/technology, workplace productivity, media and advertising, cybersecurity and digital ethics, retail, emergency response, manufacturing, gender, mixed reality, infrastructure, and sustainability.
Although these domains varied widely, several shared patterns emerged.
The most consistent pattern was that users preferred AI systems that supported their decisions without dominating them.
In HR and technology contexts, users responded strongly to the level of AI control.
Smith et al. [23] found that participants who chose to view optional AI advice were more likely to align with it, although optional access reduced alignment overall compared with mandatory advice.
text.formatted: Smith et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> found that participants who chose to view optional AI advice were more likely to align with it, although optional access reduced alignment overall compared with mandatory advice.

text.text: Signal strength or fit showed no significant effect on convergence, unlike the ability to choose whether to view the AI advice.
Ling et al. [38] found that human-led and balanced screening structures were perceived as fairer than AI-led structures, especially when applicants were rejected.
text.formatted: Ling et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> found that human-led and balanced screening structures were perceived as fairer than AI-led structures, especially when applicants were rejected.

text.text: These findings show that perceived fairness and acceptance are shaped by control, responsibility, and the user's ability to understand the decision process.
Similar patterns appeared in creative and retail contexts.

Madathil [48] found that advertisements created through human-AI collaboration were rated more positively than fully AIgenerated advertisements, with higher perceived creativity, stronger brand morality, and lower AI anxiety.
text.formatted: Madathil <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[48]</ref> found that advertisements created through human-AI collaboration were rated more positively than fully AIgenerated advertisements, with higher perceived creativity, stronger brand morality, and lower AI anxiety.

text.text: Batra et al. [34] showed that usage intention increased when users perceived both high automation and high personal control.
text.formatted: Batra et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> showed that usage intention increased when users perceived both high automation and high personal control.

text.text: Li and Kang [49] found that human-centered AI in retail could support personalization and trust, although users could also blame AI more strongly when service failures occurred.
text.formatted: Li and Kang <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref> found that human-centered AI in retail could support personalization and trust, although users could also blame AI more strongly when service failures occurred.

text.text: These findings suggest that users may accept advanced AI capabilities when they feel that human values, control, and accountability remain visible.
Explainability and transparency were also important across the smaller domains.
Shulner-Tal et al. [22] found that fairness perceptions in algorithmic decision-making were shaped by system characteristics, personality characteristics, and demographic characteristics.
text.formatted: Shulner-Tal et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> found that fairness perceptions in algorithmic decision-making were shaped by system characteristics, personality characteristics, and demographic characteristics.

text.text: Certification-based and sensitivity-based explanations improved perceived fairness, while demographicbased explanations reduced fairness perceptions and certification stamps alone had no significant effect.
Molina and Sundar [30] found that trust in AI content moderation increased when users had interactive transparency and could provide feedback on system rules.
text.formatted: Molina and Sundar <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> found that trust in AI content moderation increased when users had interactive transparency and could provide feedback on system rules.

text.text: Schmitt et al. [44] found that AI support significantly improved misinformation detection accuracy and increased subjective ratings such as trust and usefulness, while free-text explanations introduced a risk of blind trust.
text.formatted: Schmitt et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref> found that AI support significantly improved misinformation detection accuracy and increased subjective ratings such as trust and usefulness, while free-text explanations introduced a risk of blind trust.

text.text: These findings show that explanations can improve user perception, but they need to be evaluated against actual task outcomes.
The presentation of AI also mattered.
Sánchez Olszewski [55] found that participants were less likely to agree with AI when it appeared human-like, compared with robot-like or generic AI identities, in a hiring context.
text.formatted: Sánchez Olszewski <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref> found that participants were less likely to agree with AI when it appeared human-like, compared with robot-like or generic AI identities, in a hiring context.

text.text: Li and Kang [49], in a retail context, found more positive responses to humancentered AI that appeared personalized and attentive, compared with machine-centered AI that appeared more task-oriented and mechanical.
text.formatted: Li and Kang <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref>, in a retail context, found more positive responses to humancentered AI that appeared personalized and attentive, compared with machine-centered AI that appeared more task-oriented and mechanical.

text.text: These findings suggest that anthropomorphic or human-like AI design does not have one fixed effect.
Its value depends on task context, user expectations, and the risk associated with the decision.
Overall, the smaller domains supported the same broader pattern found in healthcare, education, and transportation.
Users were more likely to trust, accept, and use AI when they retained meaningful control, understood the AI's role, and perceived the system as fair and useful.
Systems that were overly dominant, unclear, or difficult to challenge were more likely to create resistance, anxiety, or overreliance.
Across the reviewed studies, HCAI and HAX evaluation depended on both task outcomes and user experience outcomes.
Many AI systems improved accuracy, speed, consistency, or decision quality, yet these gains did not always lead to stronger trust, satisfaction, usability, lower workload, or perceived control.
This pattern shows that performance outcomes and human experience outcomes need to be evaluated in relation to each other.
Another cross-domain pattern concerned the role of AI in the interaction.
Human-led AI support appeared most often in high-stakes settings where users retained final authority.
Collaborative AI appeared in tasks that required shared control, feedback, or adaptation during the interaction.
AI-led support appeared mainly as part of mixed-role systems, especially in dynamic settings where risk or task demands changed over time.
These findings show that AI role is an important factor for comparing HCAI and HAX studies across domains.
Domain context also shaped the outcomes that received the most attention.
Healthcare studies emphasized accuracy, reliability, expertise, and overreliance.
Education studies emphasized engagement, scaffolding, ownership, and learning.
Transportation studies emphasized safety, timing, modality, trust calibration, and user control.
The remaining domains emphasized fairness, transparency, adoption, creativity, and acceptance.
These patterns show that similar HCAI and HAX concerns appear across domains, while evaluation priorities vary based on users, risks, and task demands.
IV.

DISCUSSION This review synthesized 44 empirical studies on HCAI and HAX across multiple application domains and used this evidence to connect design principles, AI roles, measurement choices, and human outcomes within a single synthesis structure.
The findings show that HCAI and HAX are closely connected areas of work.
HCAI provides the values and design goals that guide AI system design, and HAX provides evidence about user interaction, system use, and measurable outcomes.

This structure helps clarify which design concerns appear across domains, which outcomes have empirical support, and where future frameworks need stronger links between human-centered values and measurable interaction outcomes.
Across the reviewed studies, HCAI and HAX research has moved beyond broad design principles toward empirical evaluation of human outcomes.
The review also shows continued fragmentation across domains, measures, and interaction contexts.
The reviewed studies used both objective and subjective measures to evaluate human-AI interaction.
Objective measures most often focus on task performance, including accuracy, error reduction, completion time, and decision quality.
Across domains, AI assistance was often associated with improved objective performance, especially in tasks involving diagnosis, classification, detection, information search, and decision support.
These findings suggest that AI can support human performance when it helps users process complex information, identify patterns, or focus on task-relevant cues.
Subjective measures showed more variation.
Trust, satisfaction, usability, and workload changed based on the design of the AI system, the clarity of its output, the user's level of control, and the task context.
This variation is important because a system can improve performance while still creating a poor user experience.
AI explanations may increase trust and perceived usefulness, yet they can also increase mental workload when users need to process too much information under time pressure.
This pattern suggests that HCAI and HAX evaluations should include both performance outcomes and user experience outcomes.
A system should not be considered human-centered only because it improves accuracy or efficiency.
It also needs to support appropriate trust, clear understanding, manageable workload, and meaningful user control.
The workload findings are especially important for future evaluation.
AI systems are often designed to reduce cognitive demand, but the reviewed studies show that this benefit is not automatic.
Explanations, alerts, and adaptive cues can reduce workload when they are clear and timely.
They can increase workload when they are too frequent, too complex, or poorly matched to the user's task.
Future studies should therefore evaluate workload as a sign of whether AI information is being integrated smoothly into human cognition and action, not just as a general measure of task difficulty.

The reviewed frameworks were organized into eight categories: automation and human control, initiative dynamics, affective and engagement orientation, cognitive support, fairness, trust, personalization and adaptivity, and technology adoption with human performance.
Among these categories, automation and human control appeared most often.
This emphasis reflects a central issue in HCAI: AI systems should improve human capability while preserving human oversight and responsibility.
Initiative dynamics also emerged as a key framework concern.
The order of human and AI input can shape performance, trust, and responsibility.
When AI acts early in the task, it may increase efficiency by reducing the user's initial effort, but it may also shape the user's later judgment.
When humans act early in the task, they may remain more engaged, but the process may require more time and effort.
Future frameworks should treat initiative as a design choice rather than a fixed feature of AI systems.
The same AI capability can produce different outcomes depending on whether it advises, critiques, initiates, or responds.
Affective, engagement, and cognitive categories show that HCAI and HAX are not limited to performance and control.
AI systems can influence motivation, emotional response, perceived cooperation, and critical reasoning.
Engagementoriented systems may be helpful in education and public-facing contexts, while cognitive support may be especially important in high-stakes decision-making.
These benefits still need to be balanced with workload and efficiency.
Features that encourage reflection can reduce overreliance, but they may also slow users down or increase mental effort.
Fairness and trust were also important framework categories.
Fairness was especially visible in HR and algorithmic decisionmaking contexts, where AI-supported decisions can affect employment and access to opportunity.
Trust appeared across many domains and was closely tied to transparency, reliability, and control.
Overtrust can lead users to accept incorrect AI outputs, while undertrust can prevent users from benefiting from helpful AI support.
These findings support the need for frameworks that treat trust as an outcome to be calibrated, not simply increased.
Personalization, adaptivity, and technology adoption were less represented.
This gap is important because AI systems are increasingly designed to adapt to users and operate in real-world settings.
Future HCAI and HAX frameworks should give more attention to long-term use, user adaptation, and implementation in realistic environments.
Without this attention, frameworks may remain difficult to apply outside controlled studies.
The reviewed studies showed that AI roles can be organized into human-led AI support, human-AI collaborative support, AI-led support, and mixed-role systems.
Human-led AI support appeared most often.
This pattern likely reflects the current use of AI in high-stakes domains, where humans remain responsible for final decisions.
In healthcare, for example, AI commonly supported diagnosis, treatment planning, and clinical judgment, while clinicians retained final authority.
This structure respects existing accountability and safety expectations while allowing AI to surface patterns that humans may miss.
Explainability was especially important in human-led AI support.
When humans are final decision-makers, they need enough information to judge whether AI recommendations are reliable.
However, explainability is not always beneficial by itself.
The effects of explanations depend on format, timing, user expertise, task complexity, and workload.
Future research should move beyond asking whether explanations help and should examine which explanation formats help which users under which task conditions.
Human-AI collaborative support appeared when tasks required shared activity, ongoing feedback, or adaptive control.
In these systems, AI did more than provide recommendations.
It helped coordinate the task, respond to user input, or adjust support based on context.
This role is especially relevant for surgery, transportation, emergency response, and collaborative learning, where interaction unfolds over time and conditions can change quickly.
AI-led support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems rather than as a stand-alone role.
This pattern suggests that most empirical HCAI and HAX research is not focused on full replacement of human users.
Instead, studies often examine systems where AI shifts between advising, collaborating, and acting based on task demands or risk.
This finding is important for future framework development because it shows that AI role should be treated as dynamic.
A system may need to advise during routine conditions, collaborate during complex tasks, and intervene during emergencies.
Healthcare was the largest domain in the review.
The main healthcare applications were decision support, diagnostic support, surgical assistance, and knowledge adoption.
AI support often improved accuracy, consistency, and efficiency, especially when paired with explainable AI.
Healthcare also showed clear risks related to overreliance, explanation burden, and user expertise.
Novices often benefited more from AI support, but they were also more vulnerable to incorrect AI outputs.
Experts were sometimes slower when working with AI, but they were less affected by errors.
These findings suggest that healthcare AI should be designed around user expertise, clinical responsibility, and safeguards against erroneous recommendations.
Education studies showed that AI was most useful when it supported active engagement and task-relevant scaffolding.
AI systems that provided feedback, feedforward, partnership, or adaptive guidance were more effective than systems that only delivered passive information.
At the same time, some forms of scaffolding reduced ownership or created dependence.
Future education research should examine whether AI support improves long-term learning and skill development.
Transportation studies emphasized adaptive interfaces, multimodal communication, user control, trust calibration, and explainable AI.
These concerns reflect the time-sensitive and safety-related nature of transportation tasks.
Adaptive interfaces can improve safety and comfort when they provide timely and clear support, but they can create frustration when they intervene unexpectedly or reduce user control.
Multimodal cues also need to be designed around urgency, driver state, and task demands.

Future transportation research should examine shared control and multimodal communication under more realistic edge cases, such as poor weather, sensor failure, construction zones, or unexpected system limitations.

Other domains, including HR, workplace productivity, media, digital ethics, retail, emergency response, manufacturing, mixed reality, infrastructure, and sustainability, showed a recurring preference for meaningful human control.
Users were more willing to accept AI advice when they could choose whether to view it, reject it, or override it.
These domains also showed that explainability can improve subjective outcomes, while objective performance gains may vary by explanation type, task context, and the risk of blind trust.
This gap between subjective and objective outcomes is important because explanations may make users feel more confident without improving their decision accuracy.
Future XAI research should therefore evaluate both perceived usefulness and actual decision quality.
Across domains, one repeated finding was that humancentered AI depends on fit between the AI role, the task, the user, and the risk level.
Healthcare requires reliability and safeguards against overreliance.
Education requires engagement and learning support.
Transportation requires timing, modality, and trust calibration.
HR and other decision contexts require fairness, transparency, and control.
These differences show that HCAI principles can transfer across domains, but their implementation and evaluation need to reflect domain-specific risks and user needs.
This review has several limitations.
The review included only studies with empirical experiments, and thus conceptual papers, perspective papers, and design guidelines without empirical data were not included.
This decision helped focus the synthesis on measurable outcomes, but it may have excluded important theoretical contributions.
The review also included only articles written in English, which may introduce language bias.
In addition, although the search followed a systematic procedure across multiple databases and grey literature sources, some relevant studies may not have been captured.
Finally, the included studies varied widely in domain, task, AI type, sample, and evaluation method, which limited direct comparison across studies.
This systematic review synthesized empirical evidence on HCAI and HAX across 44 studies and multiple application domains.
Its main contribution is the integration of design principles, AI roles, and outcome measures into a cross-domain structure for evaluating HCAI and HAX.
The review connected design principles, AI roles, evaluation measures, and human outcomes within one synthesis structure.
Across studies, AI support was often associated with improved objective task performance, including accuracy, efficiency, consistency, and decision quality.
Subjective outcomes were more variable and depended on transparency, explanation design, user control, workload, and task fit.
The findings show that HCAI and HAX evaluations should report both objective and subjective outcomes.
Performance gains alone are not enough to show that an AI system is humancentered.
Human-centered evaluation should also examine whether users understand the system, trust it appropriately, retain meaningful control, manage workload, and remain able to question AI outputs.
This review also shows that AI roles matter.
Human-led AI support was most common, especially in high-stakes domains.
Collaborative AI appeared in tasks that required shared activity or adaptive support.
AI-led support appeared mainly in mixedrole systems where AI involvement changed with task demands or risk.
Future HCAI and HAX frameworks should more clearly describe the role of AI and link each role to measurable human outcomes.
Future research should validate HCAI and HAX principles in more realistic settings, with diverse users, longer study periods, and higher-fidelity AI systems.

Stronger links are needed between human-centered values, interaction design, and measurable outcomes so that future frameworks can guide AI systems that are effective, understandable, trustworthy, and safe in real use.
